title: Heart of the Community

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For many New Zealanders, their earliest memories of childhood independence will have been the Saturday morning walk down to the local dairy to buy a newspaper for their parents, with the understanding that they could spend the change on sweets. Dairies were where all the maths they were learning at school suddenly made sense. And dairies have long been part of the nation's creative life: children in local films inevitably gather at the dairy; playwright Jacob Rajan interwove the Indian love story of the Taj Mahal among the shelves of Krishnan's Dairy; and then there is the famous book for children, Hairy Maclary from Donaldson's Dairy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It is a distinctive trait of New Zealand, the use of the word 'dairy' to mean a corner store. The Encyclopedia of New Zealand reveals that the term began as 'dairy-produce sellers' because they were once the only shops allowed to sell milk, cream, cheese and so on. 'The term 'dairy' only became commonly applied to small grocery stores from the late 1930s,' reads the Encyclopedia entry. 'Before then a small shop selling groceries would have been called a 'cash grocer'.' In 1945 a law was passed that put an end to most shops opening on Saturdays. Dairies, however, were able to be open outside of normal trading hours (Saturdays and evenings). They also expanded their range of goods.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whatever good fortunes dairies once enjoyed, however, have been thoroughly reversed by deregulation and the arrival of new forms of competition. The threat has not only come from the spread of supermarkets after the 1950s, as is frequently assumed; it was actually the grocery stores that were really affected by that development. But more recently, as supermarkets have extended their opening hours and stocked more convenience items, they have eaten away at the dairy's former advantages. Meanwhile today's retail space is becoming increasingly crowded with superettes, minimarts and petrol-station food courts, all of which are able to call on better resources than the humble family-owned dairy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tim Morris, a retail market analyst, says shop formats are constantly being replaced by new ones. You can blame the decline of both the tobacconist shop and the confectionery shop at least in part on the dairy, for instance. But he adds that while the profits made by dairies have been squeezed, the traditional dairy still has a future. 'There was a massive crunch in the numbers of dairies at one stage, but the numbers now are either flat or actually up a little.' Morris says that while the names used might differ, the basic concept embodied in the corner dairy is international. 'There is a permanent, universal demand by humans for a small convenience store... 'I want a cold drink... I want a newspaper, and I want to be able to walk to get it.' That demand is not dying anywhere.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nonetheless, opening a dairy was never a ticket to wealth, so why do people do it? For a start, barriers to entry are low; that is one reason why many new immigrants, who seldom have large sums to invest, open dairies. A 1994 study found that of 269 dairies in central and suburban Auckland, 227 were owned by immigrant families. Dairies also tend to be well situated within their neighbourhoods and, as in real estate, exactly which street a retailer is on will make all the difference. Social trends such as ageing populations are also in their favour. Retailers like dairies that are located close to home will always appeal to seniors, so are certain to be busy. Finally, the increase in women in the workforce and the pressured pace of contemporary life favour the kind of time-saving convenience offered by the dairy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Suresh Patel says he opened his first dairy after emigrating from India. He has owned five at various times including the current one in the suburb of Hoon Hay because it promised a better future for his family than if he had worked for a weekly wage. But that requires being open for seven days a week and, when you factor in restocking and cleaning, working 14-hour days. Not that Suresh is complaining. After attending university and graduating with a Bachelor of Commerce back in India, it has been his dream to own his own business. Recently, when there was a power cut, he arrived early at his Hoon Hay shop and found a long queue at the door. The electronic till was down and few had cash, so Suresh took them on trust, urging them to stock up on batteries and other essentials and repay him when they could. He enjoys the close relationship he has with his customers most of all. 'I like to know everybody. You need to smile, to talk to them and look after them.' Colin Johnson, owner of Johnson's grocery in Colombo Street, would no doubt agree. Johnson's is a traditional neighbourhood grocery store with a remarkable history - it will celebrate its 100th anniversary next year. To help the business survive, Colin has concentrated on stocking the sorts of things that people cannot find anywhere else, so to buy these specialities his regulars are prepared to come from all over the city. They all seem to have that sense of ownership many New Zealanders associate with the corner dairy.
